https://www.politico.eu/article/israel-f.text: The U.K., Australia and Canada on Friday called Israel’s decision not to pursue a criminal investigation into the deadly 2024 strike on a World Central Kitchen convoy “shameful.” The three governments said in a joint statement that “announcing this decision on World Humanitarian Day was particularly egregious,” adding that they had spent more than two years pressing Israel to examine the attack and hold those responsible to account. “This decision is both too little, and too late. The victims of this incident and their families deserve justice and accountability, and we will continue to seek answers on their behalf,” they added. Poland’s foreign ministry said in a post on X that it “does not accept the perpetrators’ evasion of legal and moral responsibility” and stressed that prosecutors in Przemyśl are still looking into the matter. Warsaw also demanded Israel provide “all necessary clarifications and materials” requested by Polish investigators. Israeli drones struck the World Central Kitchen convoy as it delivered food to civilians in Gaza, killing three Britons, an Australian, Soból, a dual U.S.-Canadian citizen and a Palestinian on April 1, 2024. The Israel Defense Forces described the attack at the time as a serious mistake and failure and pledged a thorough probe. Closing the case this week, the IDF said it determined “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident.” “Partnership requires mutual respect,” Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski wrote on X Thursday evening, warning that the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and lack of accountability for the IDF’s “excessive use of force” were undermining public support “even in pro-Israel nations.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dw.com/en/threatening-letter.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5M55t Kashmiri Hindus, known locally as Pandits, have long complained of a lack of security [FILE: June 2022] Image: Channi Anand/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A new wave of threatening letters targeting Kashmiri Pandits has deepened fears among those who have returned to the region as civil servants under an Indian government federal rehabilitation scheme. Kashmiri Pandits are members of the Hindu minority community who fled the Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley during a militant uprising in the 1990s. The latest letters, which surfaced in the last week of August, named several employees. The letters also included their addresses, vehicle registration numbers and phone numbers. Personal details exposed "Similar threat letters surfaced in early August, but the latest contains our Jammu residential address, vehicle and phone numbers, which have also been shared on social media," Anil Koul, a government employee, told DW, urging authorities to investigate the source of the leak. The letters have been attributed to a little-known group calling itself the United Liberation Council, which security officials suspect could be a front for the Pakistan -based Islamist militant outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba. The group reportedly first surfaced in July, when it released a poster marking the death anniversary of a former militant commander. Authorities have yet to confirm the letters' authenticity or the existence of the group behind them. The latest letters also distinguish between Pandits who never left the Valley — and are therefore "safe" — and those recruited under New Delhi's rehabilitation program, who are accused of working for "masters" outside Kashmir. The fresh threats have also triggered a political row. Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (JKNC) president and former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, called them a "conspiracy" aimed at delaying the restoration of statehood, which the region lost in 2019 . Abdullah also questioned why Hindu officers from outside the region were not facing similar threats. His remarks drew sharp criticism from Kashmiri Pandit groups and the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which accused him of being insensitive to the community's fears. Familiar fears Government records show 44,167 Kashmiri migrant families registered as having left since 1990 citing security concerns, of which 39,782 were Hindu. For Pandit community representatives, however, the latest threats are part of a much longer security problem. Sanjay Tickoo, president of the Kashmiri Pandit Struggle Committee (KPSS), said the threats should be viewed against the backdrop of targeted killings and repeated security concerns faced by Pandit government employees in the Valley. He blames security lapses and says repeated meetings with officials since a wave of killings in 2022 have failed to resolve their concerns. "Since 2022, meetings have resulted in nothing," Tickoo told DW. He also wondered how those making the threats have access to employees' personal details. "How are these details being posted on social media?" Tickoo asked. Targeted killings have occurred sporadically in the years since. At least seven Kashmiri Pandits were killed by militants during a spike in violence between 2020 and 2022 . One of the starkest cases was that of Rahul Bhat, a Pandit revenue official who was shot dead inside his government office in Budgam in May 2022. The last confirmed targeted killing of a Kashmiri Pandit was in October 2022, when Puran Krishan Bhat, an orchard farmer, was shot dead in Shopian district. Former Jammu and Kashmir police chief S P Vaid described the latest threats as part of a familiar militant playbook. "There is nothing new in this," Vaid told DW, calling it "a ploy by Pakistan to Islamize society." He said similar tactics had been used against migrant workers in the Valley. The difference, this time, is the precision of the threats. Personal data that should not have been easily accessible has been made public, and no clear explanation of how it was leaked has been provided. Kashmir: Fears dampen celebrations at Hindu festival To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The return dilemma The KPSS estimates roughly 6,500 Pandits who never left the Valley, along with another 4,000 who have returned as government employees under a federal rehabilitation scheme, live in India-administered Kashmir. But the reintegration of those who fled decades ago has proved challenging. Rahul Pandita, a journalist and author of "Our Moon Has Blood Clots: A Memoir of a Lost Home in Kashmir," said the government's record on rehabilitation was inadequate. "The BJP has had no rehabilitation policy for Kashmiri Hindus," Pandita told DW, arguing that the government employees in the Valley had returned under a policy introduced during the previous government of former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh. Some land has been returned and cases of killings have been investigated, he said, but "it is too little and too late." Pandita said the bigger problem was that no government could guarantee a completely secure environment for a mass return. "No matter what the government does, the situation will never be conducive enough for the Pandits to return," he said, arguing that as long as Islamist militancy exists in the region , Kashmiri Hindus would still be targeted. "It's for them then to decide if they are willing to take such a risk," he said. Beyond government employees, some Pandits who have returned and established businesses in the Valley are already living there quietly, Pandita said. "That is the best-case scenario for Kashmiri Pandits in Kashmir Valley," he said. Pandits accuse the government in New Delhi of not doing enough to protect them from alleged Islamist threats Image: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/picture alliance Security beyond protection Sushobha Barve, executive secretary of the Center for Dialogue and Reconciliation, said the latest threats expose a wider security paradox. "Despite claims of normalcy, a tiny group of active militants has successfully disrupted the lives of migrant families. Breaking the cycle of panic is essential," Barve told DW. She said there was also growing political frustration over the delay in restoring Jammu and Kashmir's statehood, arguing that this grievance cut across the region. Amitabh Mattoo, an academic and professor of international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University who has written extensively on Kashmir, said any return of Kashmiri Pandits had to be both secure and dignified. "The state has an essential role in ensuring their physical security and in protecting their property, cultural and other legitimate rights. But security measures alone will not suffice," Mattoo told DW. "A sustainable return will also require patient reconciliation, engagement with local civil society, and the gradual rebuilding of inter-community trust and social and economic ties."
